mappings.note: Pure substitution: evaluate 9x+7 at x=3 and judge the result. That is the 'uses it to predict a term' half of LO-2, not the degree question of C-2.1-LO-1.
Turns on what a=0 does to the DEGREE of ax+b (linear becomes constant). C-2.1-LO-2 is about whether a thing is a polynomial at all, which is never in doubt here.
Names 7x-4 as linear of degree 1 from the highest power. Sibling LO-2 would need a non-polynomial distractor tested on exponents; the distractors here are degree names.
Builds 4x+30 from a priced context (per-unit cost plus fixed cost) -- a linear-growth model. Not LO-2: there is no table or pattern, the rule comes from the situation.
The discriminator among the four options is degree: only 4x+16 has highest power 1. The perimeter dressing is incidental, so LO-1 rather than the modelling LO-3.
Fixed charge plus per-km rate written as 50+12x: a linear-growth model of a real situation. Distractors punish mixing up rate and constant, not degree, so not C-2.1-LO-1.

Competency, not an LO: the expression wanted is 4x+5y+3, linear in TWO variables. Every LO under C-3.2 is written for a univariate linear polynomial; the competency text explicitly covers two-variable situations.
Models the fencing length as 2x+16 from a geometric context. Not C-8.1-LO-5: nothing is asked about interpreting the 2 or the 16.
Both claims tested are about degree and the coefficient of x in 5-2x, which is LO-1's 'identifies the degree ... from the highest power'. No modelling or graph is involved.
A quantity rising by a fixed 8 from a starting value x -- the simplest linear-growth model. Not LO-2, since no pattern of successive differences is presented.
Asks which of four SITUATIONS a linear polynomial can model (area, cube volume and a product are rejected). That is LO-3's modelling judgement, applied in reverse.

Competency, not an LO: the item tests subtraction of like terms in (5x+8)-(2x+3). None of this chapter's eight outcomes covers operations on polynomials -- a genuine gap in the frame -- and C-3.2 is the nearest algebra competency.
A table of values is given and the rule 3x+4 must be written -- exactly LO-2. LO-1 would be the right code if the question stopped at 'are the differences constant?'.
Asks only what the constant term 100 MEANS in the billing situation -- intercept interpretation, LO-5. It does not ask for a value, so not LO-2.
Disproving 'every polynomial in x is linear' needs a degree-2 counterexample, so the point being tested is degree. C-2.1-LO-2 is not in play: all four options are polynomials.

Competency: the question reads the x-axis crossing off the graph of 2x-6. LO-5 covers only slope and the Y-intercept, and LO-4 is about drawing the line; the x-intercept has no outcome of its own in this chapter.
Competency: like-term arithmetic on 6x+5-(2x-3), the sign of the bracketed constant being the whole point. As with item 12, no LO in this chapter covers polynomial addition or subtraction.
The model is handed over; all that is required is P(5) from p(x)=10x+30 -- LO-2's 'uses it to predict'. Not LO-3, which would require building the rule.
Assertion and reason are both about the highest power of the variable naming a polynomial linear, which is LO-1 almost word for word.

Competency: the item hinges on solving 3x-12=0 and checking the claimed zero -4. This chapter has no outcome about the zero of a polynomial, so the competency's 'single polynomial equations' is the honest citation.
Corrects 'quadratic because it has two terms' by appealing to the highest power -- degree identification, LO-1, not the polynomial/non-polynomial test of LO-2.
Competency: requires solving 2x-10=0 and 5x-25=0 and comparing the zeros. No LO in this chapter names the zero of a polynomial.
Given p(0)=-4 and a constant increase of 3 per unit, write the rule 3x-4 -- LO-2's 'writes the rule of a linear pattern in the form ax+b'. Not LO-5: no graph and no situation to interpret.

The misconception corrected is that the constant term -3 of M(n)=8n-3 is the first output; the fix is that -3 is the value at n=0, i.e. the intercept, and the domain starts at n=1. That is intercept interpretation in the situation, LO-5, not the prediction clause of LO-2.
Competency: the stem says 'without drawing the graph', so this is solving 2x-6=0 algebraically, not reading a graph (which would be C-8.1).
Part (c) asks what the 15 and the 40 represent in the delivery context -- slope and intercept interpretation, LO-5. The P(6) computation is subordinate to that.
Part (a) is 'is 7x-5 a polynomial at all?', which is LO-2; parts (b) and (c) then ask for degree and constant term, which is LO-1. Both are genuinely tested, so both are cited.
The sequence 11,16,21,26 at x=0,1,2,3 is turned into 5x+11 and then used to predict P(8) -- LO-2 end to end. LO-1 stops at recognising constancy, which part (c) only refers back to.

Parts (a) and (b) solve 4x-20=0 (no zero-of-a-polynomial LO exists here, so competency C-3.2); part (c) asks what that zero means on the graph, which is the graph-reading competency C-8.1 rather than LO-5's slope and y-intercept.
Competency: recovers the coefficient a from a known zero of ax+8 by solving P(-4)=0. Coefficient recovery from a root has no LO in this chapter's frame.
Table to rule ax+b, then evaluation at 0 and 10 -- LO-2. (The printed answer key is wrong; see the report. The mapping follows what the question asks, not the key.)
Builds the fare model 15x+50 from the situation (LO-3) and then part (d) asks why that polynomial is linear, which is the degree argument of C-2.1-LO-1. Both halves carry marks.
Competency: evaluation, solving p(x)=q(x) for x, and the zeros of both polynomials. The equating of two linear polynomials is a single-equation solve, and zeros have no LO here.

Competency, chosen deliberately: two conditions p(2)=7 and p(5)=16 give simultaneous linear equations in a and b, which the C-3.2 text names explicitly. LO-2 assumes the pattern is read off a table, not solved for.
The whole item turns on a=0 collapsing ax+b to a constant polynomial and on the a!=0 condition for degree one -- LO-1. The algebra 3a+b=7a+b is only the vehicle.

The error to be corrected is misreading the constant term -2 as the first tower's height, i.e. intercept interpretation (LO-5); parts (b) and (d) then use H(n)=5n-2 to predict and to invert (LO-2). Domain restriction to n>=1 is what LO-5 calls interpreting in the situation being modelled.
Competency: recover a from B(4)=29, then find the zero -9/5 and argue that it has no package-count meaning. Both the coefficient recovery and the zero fall outside this chapter's LO set.

F(n)=500-35n is linear DECAY, which LO-3 names directly ('a falling resale value'), and the item asks about direction, domain and the largest admissible n. Not LO-2: the rule is given, not derived from a pattern.

Competency: pure vocabulary -- what an algebraic expression is made up of. C-2.1-LO-2 would imply the whole-number-exponent test, which this stem never applies, so forcing the LO would misreport what was assessed.

Competency for the same reason as qid:706547: variable vs constant vs coefficient in 5x+7 is naming the parts of an expression. Not C-8.1-LO-5 -- there is no graph and no situation, even though the model answer glosses the coefficient as a rate.
States the degree of 7x+4 from the highest power -- LO-1 exactly. Nothing about whether it is a polynomial, so not LO-2.
Degree of a non-zero constant polynomial is zero, justified by the variable appearing to power zero: a degree-identification question, LO-1.
Four polynomials, each to be given its degree and its type name (linear, quadratic, constant, cubic) -- LO-1's 'identifies the degree ... and names a polynomial of degree one as linear'.
True/false on the degree of 8x+3 being one. Degree only, so LO-1 and not LO-2.
Fill-in for the degree of 9-2x; the leading term being written second is the only subtlety. LO-1.
Matching four polynomials to their degrees 0,1,2,3 -- degree identification across types, LO-1.
Selecting the linear polynomial from a set means applying the degree-one naming rule, LO-1. No non-polynomial distractor is being screened, so not LO-2.
Definition of a linear polynomial in terms of highest power one and a!=0 -- the naming clause of LO-1.
Assertion 4x+9 is linear, reason its highest power is one: both statements are LO-1, and the item tests whether the reason explains the assertion.
'Every constant is a linear polynomial' is false on degree grounds (degree 0, not 1) -- LO-1 again, the constant/linear boundary.
Identifies m in y=mx+c as the slope. LO-5 is the only outcome in this chapter that names slope; LO-4 is about drawing the line and LO-6 about parallelism.
Computes slope 3 from the two points (1,3) and (4,12). Cited to LO-5 as the slope outcome; not C-3.2-LO-1, because no table of successive constant differences is presented.
Two steps genuinely assessed: get the slope from two points (LO-5), then write the rule y=2x+1 and verify it against the second point (LO-2's ax+b rule).
Interpreting slope zero as 'y does not change as x changes', i.e. what the slope means -- LO-5. Not LO-6: only one line is involved, so parallelism is not in question.
Fill-in naming m the slope of the line. Same outcome as qid:706559, phrased as a gap-fill.
Substitutes x=5 into y=4x-3 to predict y=17 -- the 'uses it to predict' clause of LO-2. Not LO-5: neither the 4 nor the -3 is being interpreted.
Matches four equations to their slopes, including a negative coefficient and the horizontal y=7 -- reading the slope off the form, LO-5.
Reads the y-intercept -9 from y=4x-9. LO-5 covers both slope and y-intercept; LO-4 would require the graph to be constructed.
Where y=2x+5 crosses the y-axis, answered by putting x=0: the y-intercept half of LO-5.
'y=6x passes through the origin' is a statement about the y-intercept being zero -- LO-5. Not LO-6, since no second line and no intercept change is offered.
